population.note: Simulated (fictional). 14.8% of ~262M US adults ≈ 38.8M current users, all indications (Gallup-style self-report, Aug 2028). Arithmetic: ever 21 − current 14.8 = 6.2 pp used-and-off-now; restarters currently on ≈ 7.0 pp (≈47% of current users); stopped-at-least-once = 6.2 + 7.0 = 13.2 pp = 63% of ever-users (consistent with ~one-third one-year persistence); cumulative restart among stoppers = 7.0/13.2 ≈ 53% over up to four years (above the 36–47% one-year figure, pushed up by $49–69 cash prices); cycled_off_and_on = 7.0/21 = 33%. Age bands weighted by adult population shares (≈20/33/24/23%) reproduce ~14.8%. Income thirds (18/15.5/11) average 14.8; the bottom third lags not on drug price but on visit fees, pharmacy access, uninsured status and loss of employer coverage. About 1 in 8 current users (~4.8M, ~1.8% of adults) started with BMI under 27 ('metabolic health'/longevity use). ~5.4M adults (2.1%) say they wanted the drug and have never been able to get or keep it. Pediatric ~1% of under-18s, overwhelmingly adolescents 12–17 with obesity; under-12 use remains specialist-only and still skews upper-income.

access.public_coverage: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge pilot expired on schedule Dec 2027; obesity coverage continued from Jan 2028 only through Part D plans that opted into CMS's pre-announced CMMI model, at the existing ~$245 negotiated brand rate and $50 copay, with unbranded semaglutide on many formularies at ~$60 net. Roughly 1.6M Medicare beneficiaries fill for obesity-only codes; ~6.9M more fill under diabetes/cardiac/CKD codes. Medicaid coverage for obesity varies by state; ~3.9M Medicaid enrollees on therapy, majority diabetes-coded.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India 40+ brands at ~$8–48/month; Canada generics widespread at CAD ~70–110; Brazil, Mexico and much of Southeast Asia supplied by Indian and Chinese manufacturers; generic oral semaglutide launched in India 2027. Generic semaglutide available in ~160 countries.
access.note: US 'generic' is an authorised generic: Novo Nordisk, under a 2027 patent-litigation settlement, sells unbranded semaglutide through a subsidiary and licensed distributors (Viatris, Teva) from Feb 2028 — injectable $49/month, oral $69/month cash, also via Cost Plus pharmacies. No independent ANDA generic is marketed; the compound patent still runs to ~2031–32; tirzepatide has no generic. Brand list prices unchanged (Wegovy $1,349) but irrelevant; Zepbound vials via LillyDirect ~$349–499; Foundayo $149 starter, $99–149 maintenance after Lilly's Mar 2028 cut. New starts in 2028 are ~60% oral; installed base ~55% oral. Fill shares by payer: commercial 34% (~13.2M, mostly diabetes/cardiac-coded), Medicare 22% (~8.5M), Medicaid 10% (~3.9M), cash 34% (~13.2M, incl. most of the ~4.8M non-obese users). Medicare obesity-code spend, annualised: 1.0M brand users × $245 × 12 = $2.94B + 0.6M unbranded × $60 × 12 = $0.43B ≈ $3.4B/yr, inside CBO's ≥$35B/9-yr envelope. Compounding largely priced out; residual gray market is personal importation of Indian generics and peptide 'research' vials for microdosing.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic and unbranded authorised generic)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg, Rybelsus, unbranded oral semaglutide)
GLP-1 + amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved Jan 2027)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction symptoms (tirzepatide, label update 2027)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'metabolic health' and longevity microdosing (typically 0.25–0.5 mg weekly injectable or low-dose oral) by people with BMI under 27, via telehealth wellness clinics; ~4.8M users

gambling disorder and compulsive buying — positive RCT (2028) and an APA practice advisory naming GLP-1s as an off-label adjunct; addiction psychiatrists and sportsbook-responsible-gaming referral programmes prescribe
alcohol reduction — phase 3 oral semaglutide AUD trial enrolling; widely prescribed off-label
compulsive screen use and compulsive sexual behaviour — observational and small open-label data only, heavily marketed by wellness telehealth
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
drugs.pipeline_note: Oral parity realised within the rules: a 2027 head-to-head trial showed oral semaglutide 25 mg non-inferior to weekly injectable semaglutide 2.4 mg (≈−14.8% vs −15.3% at 72 weeks); FDA updated labels to permit direct switching. No pill yet matches tirzepatide (~21%); 'parity' means parity with the injectable most people actually use. CagriSema approved Jan 2027 (~20%), modest uptake after its REDEFINE-4 miss. Retatrutide BLA filed Mar 2027, standard review, advisory committee on dysesthesia scheduled; decision expected H1 2029 — not on market. Survodutide filed Q3 2027 (obesity + MASH), under review. Amycretin phase 3 ongoing, no filing. MariTide phase 3, not on market. Compulsion indication: no FDA approval; Novo's oral semaglutide AUD phase 3 is the nearest filing (~2029). Global incretin revenue ~$95B in 2027 (volume up, US net price down sharply); 2030 forecasts cut from $150B+ to ~$120B.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Most common class effect; slightly lower on low-dose 'wellness' regimens; still the leading cause of discontinuation.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; Ozempic label 'not recommended in severe gastroparesis'.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Long-term RCTs and larger cohorts still have not confirmed causality; absolute risk low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; MDL litigation ongoing, first bellwether trials scheduled 2029.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~25–30% of weight lost is lean mass; bone-density signal replicated in two 2027 cohorts in adults 65+; concern now also attaches to normal-weight microdosers.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change; ACSM and AACE guidance recommends resistance training and protein targets; muscle-preserving adjuncts still in trials.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Conflicting cohorts; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label for semaglutide; FDA added to postmarketing section of semaglutide label 2027, no class warning.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association; anhedonia findings did not revive it.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Pooled reanalysis of maintenance-phase trial data plus a prospective SHAPS-scale registry: clinically meaningful anhedonia in ~3% of users at maintenance doses vs ~1% matched placebo (~2 pp excess, ≈780k excess cases across ~38.8M users); higher (~4–5%) at top tirzepatide doses; usually resolves within 4–8 weeks of dose reduction or stopping.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class labelling (Mar 2027) adds 'anhedonia / reduced pleasure' to Adverse Reactions with prevalence; advises dose reduction if persistent; no boxed warning. EMA followed Sep 2027.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Trial data (~two-thirds regained within a year) and real-world data still diverge; real-world regain smaller where users restart quickly at low cash prices.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; underpins chronic-therapy framing and the employer argument that cheap cash supply makes coverage unnecessary.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Iron, B12, vitamin D shortfalls reported in cohorts; strongest in older and low-income users.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects in adolescents; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Roughly six years of rigorous follow-up; still no data on decades-long or cycling use, now relevant to ~7M restarters.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements; NIH-funded cycling cohort launched 2027.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: New reports falling as $49 authorised generic undercuts compounders; residual harms from imported and 'research peptide' vials.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion finalised 2027; import alerts on unapproved semaglutide.

safety_ledger.effect: Oral contraceptive efficacy reduction (tirzepatide) and unplanned pregnancy
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Reduced oral contraceptive absorption at initiation/escalation; more salient as women 18–35 adopt via cash channels.

safety_ledger.effect: Use in people without obesity (BMI <27): long-term low-dose effects on muscle, bone and nutrition
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~4.8M users; no RCT designed for this population.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; FTC warning letters to two wellness clinics over longevity claims (2028).

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households ~28% of US households. Salty snack and confectionery volumes down ~2–3%/yr; carbonated soft drinks down ~2%; protein, fibre and small-format SKUs grow; 'GLP-1 friendly' labels ubiquitous and largely meaningless. Revenue held up better than volume via price-per-gram increases on smaller packs. JPMorgan trims its $30–55B 2030 loss range toward the upper end as cheap pills spread.

alcohol.state: US spirits volumes down ~4% in 2027 and again in 2028; heavy-drinker decline is the story. Diageo and Brown-Forman have cut US headcount and lean into non-alcoholic and premium 'occasion' bottles. Las Vegas Strip resorts report beverage revenue per occupied room down mid-single digits.

restaurants.state: Traffic roughly flat; check size per head flat to slightly down as appetisers and second drinks disappear. Smaller-plate menus, 'half' portions at full-price margin and high-acid, high-spice dishes spread. All-you-can-eat buffets close at the margin; Las Vegas buffet count keeps falling.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists continue shrinking (store closures at Torrid and DXL); mainstream retailers see size curve shift down one size; tailoring and alterations services grow.

fitness.state: Strength training is the growth category; gyms sell 'muscle insurance' packages with protein and DEXA scans; cardio-only boutique chains lose share.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage 60%→43%; most remaining plans cover only diabetes, cardiovascular, OSA or CKD codes; HR materials point employees to $49 cash. Pharmacy trend moderates to ~7% as unbranded semaglutide enters formularies. Life insurers begin asking 'current GLP-1 use' on applications, without rating it.

pharma.state: Volume up, US net price down sharply. Novo trades US brand revenue for share with its authorised generic and restructures again; Lilly holds price on tirzepatide and leads branded growth; retatrutide is the next premium bet. Indian manufacturers supply most of the world outside the US.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: In middle-class and affluent America a lean body signals nothing; a heavy body after 40 increasingly reads as a choice or a hardship — something that needs explaining. 'Are you on?' is a routine question at doctor's visits, weddings and office lunches; 'I'm off right now' is said apologetically.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Price no longer rations; time, information and coverage do. A $69 pill is trivial for the top third and a real line item for a household on $35k with no employer plan. Heaviness is concentrating, visibly, among the uninsured working poor and in rural counties without nearby pharmacies or broadband telehealth.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared plates have shrunk; hosts plan for half the food. Women 45–64 in suburban Phoenix (Chandler, Gilbert) — an early adopter cluster — describe dinner parties as 'conversation with garnish'. Church potlucks and Thanksgiving remain the places where non-users and users visibly diverge.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating app profiles add 'on/off' as a casual field; couples where one partner is on and the other off report mismatch in appetite for food, drink and going out; labelled anhedonia gives a vocabulary ('it's the dose') to some relationship complaints.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite — for food, drink, bets, shopping — is treated as a dial rather than a self. Craving is medicalised as 'noise'; the minority who report enjoying their appetite are a recognisable, slightly defensive subculture.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Labelled March 2027 at ~3% vs ~1% placebo at maintenance doses (≈2 pp excess, roughly 780k excess people nationally), higher at top tirzepatide doses, typically reversible with dose reduction. Some endocrinology and obesity-medicine clinics now add a two-question pleasure screen at maintenance visits; most primary care does not.
interior_life.framing: A labelled, uncommon side effect, handled like sexual side effects of SSRIs: mentioned at prescribing, managed by dose. Simultaneously the mechanism is the selling point for off-label gambling, shopping and drinking use — clinicians separate 'craving reduction' (wanted) from 'anhedonia' (labelled) though patients often can't.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Not systematically studied. Sales managers and commission-driven trades swap anecdotes about flat, 'fine' reps; others credit the drug with fewer snack breaks and less doomscrolling. No employer encourages or tracks it.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Comedy has a stock 'on it' persona — pleasant, unbothered. A small musician cohort publicly goes off for touring or recording. Intensity-seeking (sour candy, extreme heat, cold plunges) is now a mainstream retail category. Fantasy sports and sportsbook engagement among users dips measurably in operator data.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Labelled anhedonia is cited in couples therapy; reduced desire remains anecdotal but common enough that some partners negotiate dose timing around anniversaries and holidays.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Marginal. In two state legislatures (Ohio, New Jersey) sports-betting opponents cite the gambling RCT; operators fund responsible-gaming referral programmes that include GLP-1 prescribing. No law has passed. Commentators speculate about a calmer electorate; there is no evidence for it.

state.regulatory_posture: Unchanged in kind: pro-access, pro-speed approvals and enforcement against compounders; no new federal programme this window. FDA acted through labelling (anhedonia, oral switching) rather than restriction.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. Medicare Bridge expired Dec 2027 as scheduled; continuation depends on Part D plan opt-in to the pre-announced CMMI model. TrumpRx cash channel continues and lists the $49/$69 unbranded products.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Coverage conditioned on diabetes/cardiac/BMI codes and prior authorisation; life-insurance application questions about GLP-1 use; no adherence monitoring.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The India–US price gap that was a political fact in 2026 has largely closed for semaglutide (US $49 vs India $8–48); it persists for tirzepatide. Unbranded semaglutide API is partly sourced from Novo's Danish and North Carolina plants, insulating it from tariff disputes.

events.event: FDA adds 'anhedonia / reduced pleasure' to all incretin labels, citing ~3% incidence at maintenance doses vs ~1% on placebo; no boxed warning, dose reduction advised

Head-to-head trial finds daily oral semaglutide 25 mg non-inferior to weekly Wegovy injection at 72 weeks; FDA label update permits direct switching and pill starts overtake injection starts by year-end

Novo Nordisk settles US semaglutide patent challenges and announces an authorised generic; unbranded injectable ($49/month) and oral ($69/month) semaglutide reach pharmacies and Cost Plus in Feb 2028; Lilly cuts Foundayo maintenance cash price to $99–149

Business Group on Health survey: employer coverage for weight management to fall to 43% in 2028, with most remaining plans restricted to diabetes, cardiac and sleep-apnea codes; employers cite $49 cash availability
JAMA Psychiatry RCT: semaglutide reduces gambling days and losses in gambling disorder; APA issues practice advisory naming GLP-1s an off-label adjunct for gambling and compulsive buying
Gallup: 14.8% of US adults on an incretin drug; one in eight users started without obesity; two-thirds of adults 50–64 who are not on one say they 'get asked why'

open_tensions: A $49 authorised generic has turned access into a question of income floors, insurance and time; employers treat cheap cash as a reason to exit, and the bottom income third is falling further behind the national rate.
Craving reduction is sold for gambling, shopping and drinking while the same effect is labelled as anhedonia at ~3% — patients, clinicians and wellness telehealth draw the line in different places.

Nearly 5M people without obesity take low-dose incretins for 'metabolic health' with no trial evidence for muscle, bone or decades-long use, and ~7M adults have cycled off and on with no data on what cycling does.
Retatrutide's 2029 decision will reopen a premium injectable tier above a commodity pill, testing whether two-tier access becomes three-tier.
still_true: The US semaglutide compound patent still runs to roughly 2031–32 and there is no independent (non-licensed) FDA-approved generic semaglutide or any generic tirzepatide on the US market.
Wegovy's list price remains $1,349/month, though almost nobody pays it.
FDA's January 2026 removal of the suicidal-ideation warning from Saxenda, Wegovy and Zepbound labels stands; the effect remains classed as debunked.
Foundayo (orforglipron) remains on the market with its initial oral doses at $149–150 cash through TrumpRx and Lilly's direct channel.
India's generic semaglutide market of 40+ brands continues at roughly $8–48/month.

prose.headline: Fifty Dollars and a Pill: America Stopped Asking Who's On It. Now It Asks Why You're Not.
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028 roughly one American adult in seven takes an incretin drug, about 39 million people, and most of the new ones swallow it. The needle mattered less than anyone admitted once a 2027 head-to-head trial showed the daily semaglutide pill doing what the weekly Wegovy pen did. Pill starts passed injection starts that winter. Then the price went. Novo Nordisk, losing ground to Lilly and tired of watching Canadians and Indians buy its molecule for pocket change, settled its patent fights and began selling its own unbranded semaglutide in February 2028: forty-nine dollars a month for the pen, sixty-nine for the pill, on the shelf at Cost Plus and at the chain pharmacy beside the cough syrup. The patent still runs to the early 2030s. Wegovy's list price is still $1,349. Neither number means much any more.

Cheap supply gave employers a reason to leave. For 2028, 43 percent of large employers cover weight management, down from 60 percent two years earlier and 72 percent before that. Most of the plans that remain will pay only if a diabetes, heart or sleep-apnea code is on the chart. The HR memo says the drug is affordable now, and for many people it is. For a home health aide in rural Georgia earning $31,000 with no plan, the sixty-nine dollars is a real line item, and so are the telehealth visit, the pharmacy forty minutes away and the lab work. The bottom income third uses the drugs at about 11 percent and the top third at 18. Price used to be what kept people out. Now it's income, coverage and time. Medicare's pilot ran out on schedule at the end of 2027, and beneficiaries now depend on whether their Part D plan opted into the follow-on model. About 1.6 million are covered for obesity alone.

At the same time the drug has spread beyond the people it was approved for. About one user in eight never had obesity. They microdose through wellness clinics that talk about longevity and keep their weight-loss claims vague. In April a psychiatry trial showed semaglutide cutting gambling losses, and within weeks addiction clinics, and some sportsbooks' own responsible-gaming programmes, were prescribing it. Compulsive shopping, scrolling and sex are marketed next, on much thinner evidence.

The cost of that mechanism now appears in the prescribing information. Since March 2027 every label lists anhedonia, reduced pleasure, at about 3 percent on maintenance doses against 1 percent on placebo. It is uncommon, usually reversible with a lower dose, and handled the way SSRI sexual side effects are: mentioned once, managed quietly. Some obesity clinics ask two questions about pleasure at each refill. Most primary care offices don't ask. Users talk about "the dose" the way earlier generations talked about "my nerves".

The economy has adjusted without breaking. Snack volumes fall a couple of points a year and packs get smaller at higher prices per gram. Spirits are in real contraction, driven by heavy drinkers drinking less. On the Las Vegas Strip, beverage revenue per room is down and the buffets keep closing. Plus-size chains shut stores while tailors take in waistbands. Gyms sell muscle preservation the way they once sold weight loss.

What has changed most is the default. Among women in their late forties in Chandler or Gilbert, among executives, among anyone with a dentist and a pharmacy app, taking it is unremarkable. A heavy body past forty reads as a hardship or a decision, and either way people ask about it. "I'm off right now" is said apologetically. About seven million adults have cycled off and back on, and no one knows what a decade of that does. Retatrutide's FDA decision is due in 2029. If it is approved, a premium injection will sit above a commodity pill.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Marisol Ortega takes her pill at 5:40 a.m. with four ounces of water, then waits the thirty minutes on the edge of the tub, scrolling. The bottle says SEMAGLUTIDE TABLETS 25 MG in plain type, no brand, $69 at the Walgreens on Eastern. Her union plan stopped paying in January unless you're diabetic. She isn't.

Her husband Ray is eating cereal from the box. He quit in March. He said the pill made the Raiders boring. She didn't argue.

At the casino the shift meeting is about upselling. The beverage manager shows a chart. Tables are ordering one round and then water. Marisol carries a tray of soda waters through the pit and watches a man in a golf shirt sit at blackjack for eleven minutes, lose forty dollars, shrug and leave. Six years ago he'd have stayed till three.

On break, Dani from cocktails asks if she's still on. Marisol says yes. Dani says her sister's on it for the slots now, a doctor gave it to her through a gambling program, and she's stopped calling. Not in a bad way. Just stopped.

After work Marisol picks up her son's birthday cake, a small one. Eight people, and three of them won't eat it.

At home she finds the song from their wedding and plays it in the kitchen while Ray dries dishes. It sounds fine and she knows every word. She waits for the thing in her chest and it doesn't come.

Ray is watching her. "Dose," he says, not unkindly.

She writes it on the fridge list, under eggs: ask Dr. P about 14.
